content: The development of a suitable formulation for delivering raltegravir (RAL) to neonates began in 2018. Due to concerns about the complexity of administering the granule formulation, the Paediatric Antiretroviral Working Group recommended the use of 25-mg chewable tablets, which can also be dispersed, for infants and children older than four weeks and weighing at least 3 kg. This decision was based on in vitro data demonstrating solubility and bioequivalence between RAL chewable tablets and granules, as well as the limited availability of alternative formulations for this age group. In the updated dosing guidance, appropriate dose adjustments for RAL during rifampicin-based tuberculosis (TB) treatment are recommended. These adjustments should continue for two weeks after the completion of rifampicin-based TB treatment to account for the enzyme-inducing effects of rifampicin, which gradually diminish after discontinuation. The 2021 update to the consolidated guidelines on HIV prevention, testing, treatment, service delivery, and monitoring confirmed dosing information for children using tenofovir alafenamide (TAF). Fixed-dose combinations containing TAF were included for children weighing 25 kg or more, with a 25-mg dose when used in unboosted regimens. This aligns with dosing approved by the United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA). Studies to determine appropriate dosing for children weighing less than 25 kg are ongoing, and further information will be provided once regulatory approval is extended. The dosing annex and simplified dosing schedule will be regularly reviewed and updated as new data and formulations become available. Updated information on antiretroviral (ARV) drug dosing in children and the rationale for dose simplification is accessible via the newly developed paediatric ARV dosing dashboard. ARV drugs and formulations are available from various manufacturers, but the dosage strengths of tablets, capsules, and liquid formulations may differ from the information provided in the guidelines. Several optimal dosage forms for children are under development but have not yet received regulatory approval. National programme managers must ensure that products intended for use have received stringent regulatory approval and meet appropriate quality and stability standards. The current list of WHO-prequalified drugs and the FDA's list of approved and tentatively approved ARV drugs are available. The Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis, and Malaria also provides a policy on procurement and quality assurance. The WHO followed specific principles in developing simplified dosing tables. Age-appropriate fixed-dose combinations are preferred for any regimen if such formulations are available. Oral liquid or syrup formulations should be avoided when possible, except for neonatal treatment and prevention. Dispersible tablets or granules are the preferred solid oral dosage forms, as they can be converted into liquid at the point of use. If suitable dispersible fixed-dose combinations are unavailable and oral liquids must be used, children should transition to solid oral dosage forms as soon as possible. For newborns, oral liquid formulations are generally required for precise dosing, but switching to solid oral dosage forms is recommended as soon as feasible. When children must use adult formulations, care must be taken to avoid underdosing or overdosing. Scored tablets are preferred to ensure accurate dosing, especially when using adult dosage forms. Splitting unscored tablets should be avoided, as uniform distribution of the active drug cannot be guaranteed in tablet fragments. Certain tablets, such as heat-stable lopinavir/ritonavir (LPV/r) or atazanavir/ritonavir (ATV/r), are manufactured using proprietary melt extrusion technology to stabilize heat-labile drug molecules. These tablets must not be cut, split, dissolved, chewed, or crushed, as bioavailability is significantly reduced when they are not swallowed whole. For children requiring an LPV/r-based regimen, LPV/r is available in a 40 mg/10 mg pellet or granule formulation for infants and young children. However, children weighing 10 kg or more should transition to LPV/r heat-stable tablets as soon as they can swallow tablets whole. This transition improves administration, palatability, and reduces pill burden. After the first four weeks of life, infants and children should be weighed at each clinic visit, and doses should be adjusted based on observed growth and changes in body weight. Country programmes should consider national regulatory and local availability statuses of specific dosage forms when developing national recommendations for treating children. Research is ongoing for several ARV medications to establish dosing guidance for neonates, infants, and young children. Age indications for each drug mentioned in the guidelines are based on current evidence and will be updated as new recommendations become available. For infants at least four weeks old but weighing less than 3 kg, the immaturity of renal and hepatic elimination pathways is less concerning, but uncertainty remains regarding appropriate ARV dosing for preterm and low-birth-weight infants. Pharmacokinetic data for preterm infants are available only for zidovudine (AZT), with limited data and considerable uncertainty for nevirapine (NVP), RAL, and lamivudine (3TC). LPV/r solution should not be given to preterm infants until they reach 42 weeks of gestational age due to the risk of adverse effects. The LPV/r liquid formulation requires a cold chain for transport and storage. Heat-stable LPV/r tablets must be swallowed whole and should not be split, chewed, dissolved, or crushed. Adult 200/50 mg tablets can be used for children weighing 14–<25 kg (one tablet in the morning and one in the evening) and for children weighing 25–<35 kg (two tablets in the morning and one in the evening). LPV/r pellets should not be used for infants younger than three months. More details on administering LPV/r pellets are available. The dosing schedule applies to equivalent solid dosage forms, such as LPV/r granules, which can be used from two weeks of age. However, due to constrained supply, pellets and granules should be discouraged for children weighing more than 14 kg, who should instead receive LPV/r 100/25 mg tablets. RTV oral solution dosing is based on trial data supporting its use for super-boosting in young children receiving LPV/r. RTV should only be used as a boosting agent in combination with ATV or darunavir (DRV). RAL granules are approved from birth, but their feasibility and acceptability have not been widely investigated. Concerns have been raised about administration in resource-limited settings. However, findings from a feasibility and acceptability assessment in South Africa demonstrate that administering RAL granules in rural settings is feasible with adequate training and counseling.
